analytic.title: Utilization-based Schedulability Analysis for Switched Ethernet aiming Dynamic QoS Management

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Ethernet switches are typically found in many largescale distributed real-time systems providing low-end transactions as well as bulk backbone routing to realtime applications. The FTT-SE protocol (Flexible Time-Triggered communication over Switched Ethernet) is a recent proposal to bypass the limitations of conventional switches in terms of real-time behavior while catering for growing requirements on dynamic reconfigurability and adaptability. For this end, this paper develops linear timecomplexity and memory-efficient on-line admission control tests based on utilization bounds for Rate-Monotonic and EDF scheduling on Ethernet switches using FTT-SE, which are suited for dynamic Quality of Service (QoS) management. Our analysis also has broader applicability in general periodic task sets with bounded release delays. For FTT-SE with 100Mbps links and 1500 bytes of maximum packet size, our sufficient schedulability condition achieves an utilization bound of 61% for RMS and 88% for EDF. Simulation results on randomly generated task sets demonstrate that such bounds are within 18% and 5% utilization of the ideal tests for RMS and EDF, respectively.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Ethernet switches are increasingly used in the backbone communication infrastructure of large-scale distributed real-time systems like ships, trains, aircrafts, factories and process control. These distributed real-time computing systems are required to closely interact with their physical operating environments. Such interaction not only poses timing constraints, but also requires the computing infrastructure to be able to dynamically adapt, possibly reconfiguring itself, be it for the sake of openness, e.g., new subsystems or components arrive and are connected on-line, or for the sake of efficiency, e.g., to better use network bandwidth or computing power with variable load, or even to minimize power consumption.

Therefore, Ethernet networks used in real-time systems are required to provide timely yet adaptable communication in a controlled fashion, so that the system integrity and its basic services are not compromised.

A substantial amount of work has been carried out to realize real-time communication over Ethernet [25] since its early conception in the 70s and then with the switched topology in the 90s. Commercially available Ethernet switches do have a set of helpful features in terms of improving timeliness, flexibility and traffic isolation, but they still exhibit limitations that arise from the fact that switches are designed to achieve high average throughput on Internet traffic [20] [30]. Some major drawbacks switches include are the limited number of priority levels, the use of FCFS queues and the use of shared memory that, upon overload, may cause interference across priority levels and even virtual LANs (VLANs) [26].

Many traffic control techniques have been developed to handle those limitations [25]. However, the corresponding system analysis procedures are typically either computationally heavy, such as response-time-based, or not suitable to provide a fast bandwidth management, such as the Network Calculus. Utilization-based (bandwidth-based) techniques, such as those derived from the Liu and Layland's seminal work for computational scheduling, provide a fast schedulability assessment and are better suited to carry out on-line resource distribution within a given utilization bound as needed for our target of supporting dynamic Quality-of-Service (QoS) management [13] [18].

The FTT-SE protocol (Flexible Time-Triggered communication over Switched Ethernet) [24] helps to overcome the above-mentioned limitations of standard Ethernet with a master-slave transmission control scheme op-timized for low overhead. It integrates a periodic transmission model that enables the execution of any traffic scheduling policy, e.g., priority-based schemes with arbitrary large number of priority levels, both dynamic and static, with preemption of multi-packet messages.

In this paper we use FTT-SE to provide support for adaptive and reconfigurable communication with timeliness guarantees. This paper presents a fast and efficient on-line utilization-based schedulability test for FTT-SE, which accommodates the release jitter arising due to mutual communication interference across multiple queues of the same switch. The utilization-based tests presented in this paper are applicable to the general periodic task model with bounded deferred release under both RM and EDF scheduling. The performance of the schedulability tests is evaluated using simulations. Finally, the paper describes the ongoing work on FTT-SE, and provides possible future work.

div.head: Protocols
div.p: Ethernet switches are generally tuned to provide a high throughput, as required for Internet traffic and so have poor support for timeliness [25]. Several techniques have been proposed to enhance their timing properties. One class of techniques consists of using traffic shapers in each node to limit the burstiness, and the amount of load submitted to the network, thus preventing memory overflows [23]. Master/slave techniques may also be used to achieve real-time behavior, since the master initiates every transaction and thus has complete control over the load submitted to the network. For example, the EtherCAT protocol [1] uses this technique together with specialized switches and an open-ring topology. Another example is the ETH-ERNET Powerlink protocol (EPL) [2], where a master node explicitly triggers each transaction according to a cyclic scheduling table. Transactions are always broadcast in such protocols thus they cannot exploit the available parallel forwarding paths.

Foundation HSE [4] is a layer 7 protocol, based on standard Ethernet equipment that uses a high-level communication scheduler to reduce contention by preventing devices from concurrently generating data. Similarly, Ethernet/IP [3] relies on COTS Ethernet equipment, i.e., switches, network interface cards and IP stacks. Avoiding overloads and achieving timely behavior in this case requires a careful analysis by the system designer since there are no specific run-time enforcement mechanisms.

Finally, it is also possible to enhance the switch with traffic control and scheduling capabilities. For example, Hoang et al. [19] propose the inclusion of EDF traffic scheduling and on-line admission control inside a switch. The EtheReal protocol [29] presents a similar architecture, also based on a modified Ethernet switch. PROFINET Isochronous Real Time (IRT) [5] and PEAC [10], employ a distributed cyclic time-slotting scheme encompassing a deterministic time-triggered phase and an asynchronous phase for non-real-time traffic. Recently, Wang et al. [30] proposed a new switch design that supports the features of real-time traffic, providing low latency. However, the switch configuration, such as in PROFINET-IRT, is carried out off-line and thus cannot be used for dynamic situations with arriving and departing streams and/or adaptation of the existing ones. In general, using customized switches has the disadvantage of lower (possibly no) availability of equipment and higher costs but has the potential for higher efficiency and robustness. It is thus a choice that the system architect must consider.

Comparing with the techniques above, FTT-SE follows a Master-slave approach, too, but uses polling on a cycle basis rather than message basis, reducing the overhead substantially. But, more important to our purpose, is that it is the only protocol explicitly providing guaranteed on-line traffic scheduling services, with support for arbitrary scheduling policies, while only using Ethernet COTS equipment.

div.head: Schedulability analysis
div.p: Concerning switch traffic schedulability analysis, much work has been carried out since the early 90s. Two main frameworks have been used, Network Calculus (NC) [14] [11] and response time or utilization-based analysis (RTA) [27] [19]. Song et al. [27] present a comparison of both approaches for the case of fixed-priority packet scheduling. Basically, Network Calculus is more flexible to use, relying on a more general traffic model, while providing more pessimistic delay bounds. This is the motivation for the response-time analysis for switches in [16] that also considers the impact of FCFS queues.

Despite the relatively large amount of work on network-induced delay caused by switches, particularly Ethernet switches [22][16], less attention has been devoted to utilization-based tests. Curiously, the same has happened in the real-time scheduling community, with more work dedicated recently to response-time analysis [17] [9].

The use of utilization-based tests is further complicated by the presence of FCFS queues in the switch. The works that consider such tests build upon modified switches that carry out different scheduling policies. Conversely, FTT-SE overrides the effect of FCFS queues and supports any scheduling policy on COTS switches. Thus, we will use the FTT-SE protocol to execute RM and EDF scheduling and take advantage of the respective schedulability utilization bounds with a proposed general adaptation to cope with release jitter. This will enable the deployment of dynamic QoS management, which requires such tests to perform on-line bandwidth reclamation and redistribution.

We believe that the results in this paper can also find applicability in other scopes, such as pipeline scheduling [21]. In this case, our results allow transforming precedence constraints into release jitter that can then be used to account for the schedulability of each stage independently of each other using common utilization bounds. Moreover, our results also allow eliminating the release jitter from the utilization-based tests by upper bounding its impact with utilization terms.

Finally, the recent work in [15] also includes a pseudoutilization-based schedulability test that accounts for release jitter but: i) it considers all tasks simultaneously affected by their release jitter being substantially more pessimistic than considering the maximum release jitter once for the set of tasks as in our case, and ii) does not directly reflect bandwidth.

div.head: Brief overview of FTT-SE
div.p: FTT-SE [24] follows the FTT architecture used in other protocols such as FTT-CAN (for Controller Area Network) and FTT-Ethernet (for shared Ethernet). This architecture uses a Master node to coordinate the transmissions of other nodes but uses an efficient triggering mechanism that substantially reduces the high overhead of typical master-slave solutions (Fig. 1). The communication is organized in fixed duration slots called Elementary Cycles (ECs), which are triggered by a master message called Trigger Message (TM) that contains the schedule for that EC. The periodic traffic is handled using synchronous messages, which are synchronized with the periodic traffic scheduler. The protocol also supports both real-time and non real-time aperiodic traffic, through asynchronous messages. The aperiodic traffic is managed in the background with respect to the periodic one, or within specific phases, and will not be further considered in this paper.

The traffic scheduling activity is carried out on-line and locally in the master, invoked once per EC, and the traffic schedules are disseminated by means of the TM. Typical EC duration goes from 1ms for high timing resolution to as large as desired for slow applications, further saving overhead. Since the traffic scheduling is local to one node, it is easy to enforce any kind of scheduling policy as well as perform atomic changes in the communication requirements. This last feature allows for on-line stream admission and removal under guaranteed timeliness as well as on-line bandwidth management. The protocol also enables the system designer to use arbitrary bandwidth management policies. These features are the kernel of the FTT paradigm and are the justification for the flexible attribute.
The reader is referred to [24] for a deeper discussion on the specific mechanisms of the protocol.

div.head: Communication model
div.p: The periodic scheduling model in FTT-SE considers N message streams (m i ) whose descriptors are stored in the Synchronous Requirements Table (Γ ) (1). Each stream m i is characterized by the total transmission time of each instance, C i , considering all physical layer overheads such as the inter-frame gap, the relative deadline D i , T i is the stream period, O i the offset and P r i an optional explicit priority. Both D i , T i and O i are expressed as integer numbers of ECs. S i is the sender node and R 1 i ..R ki i is the set of k i receivers (multicast model). However, in this work we will only consider the restricted model expressed in (2) with D i = T i , to prevent excessive efficiency degradation of RM and EDF schedulability utilization tests. We also assume RM and EDF priorities, for the corresponding case, as well as arbitrary release offsets.
div.formula: Γ = m i C i , D i , T i , O i , P r i , S i , R 1 i ..R ki i , i = 1..N (1)
div.p: The current implementation on COTS switches, does not support multicast/broadcast messages, i.e., each message has a single receiver R i . This is to avoid the strong degradation such messages cause in the traffic schedulability level when using COTS switches [24]. Multicast/broadcast messages will be addressed in future work.
div.formula: Γ = {m i (C i , T i , S i , R i ) , i = 1..N }(2)
div.p: Concerning C i note that the protocol automatically fragments large messages in a sequence of packets that are individually scheduled by the master. This is very useful to transmit regularly large amounts of data, e.g., video frames. As usual, each packet transmission is nonpreemptive but message transmission is fully preemptive between packets. As seen later in Section 4.2, using inserted-idle-time at the end of each cycle explicitly prevents any non-preemption effects and allows considering a fully preemptive scheduling model at an EC scale [6].
Finally, without loss of generality, we consider Γ to be sorted by ascending periods, i.e., ∀ i =j : i < j ⇒ T i < T j .

div.head: Window confinement
div.p: The FTT-SE scheduler strictly confines the periodic traffic to a Synchronous Window of duration LSW , which allows bounding the bandwidth assigned to this type of traffic with respect to the other types. This means that when a message cannot be fully transmitted within this window, it is kept in the ready queue and the scheduling for that EC in that link is suspended and resumed in the following one, as illustrated in Fig. 2. This property prevents window overrun but introduces idle-time that must be accounted for in the analysis.

The effect of such inserted-idle-time (IIT) has been thoroughly studied in [6] for fixed-priorities scheduling and [7] for EDF. Therein, it was shown that when scheduling within a periodic partition of length S and period E, as long as the message transmission time C i is inflated with a compensation factor, becoming C i , as in (3), with X being the maximum IIT upper-bounded by the maximum packet length, any schedulability analysis for preemptive scheduling with fixed or dynamic priorities applies.
div.formula: C i = C i E S -X(3)
div.p: When considering utilization-based tests, the compensation factor can be applied to reduce the utilization least upper bound while the transmission times C i are kept unchanged as shown in (4). We will include this compensation factor in the analysis proposed in this paper.
div.formula: C i T i ≤ U lub × S -X E(4)

div.head: Deferred release in the downlinks
div.p: Transmissions in the downlinks are causal with respect to those in the uplinks and thus must always occur after them, at least an amount of time ε. This means that, if a set of packets arrive close to the end of the synchronous window at a given queue, their transmission might extend beyond the end of that window, even if the total load in that downlink takes much less than LSW (see the downlink of Node C in Fig. 3). See for example the case of Node A. It sends message m 1 to some other node not shown, m 2 to Node B and m 3 to Node C. If T 1 , T 2 and T 3 are different from each other, some times message m 3 will suffer interference from m 1 and/or m 2 and other times will not suffer interference. This interference appears only indirectly at the downlink of Node C, the destination of message m 3 , because of its deferred release caused by the transmissions of m 1 and m 2 in the same uplink. Thus, m 3 arrives irregularly at the downlink with a release jitter J 3 that is bounded by the maximum interference it can suffer (in this case, C 1 + C 2 ). Therefore, when constraining the traffic in the downlinks to LSW it is necessary not only to account for the transmission duration but also for the respective transmission instants. The FTT-SE scheduler handles this for the downlinks in each EC.

The causality phenomenon also extends beyond this intra-EC level. In fact, it is possible that a message in one uplink suffers interference enough to be delayed several ECs from its exact periodic activation. As a consequence, that message in its downlink might appear with a deferred release jitter (J i ) of several ECs. The amount of time that a message can be deferred in a downlink is directly related to the interference that it can suffer in the respective uplink from messages that are sent to different destinations.

div.head: Scheduling multiple links simultaneously
div.p: The scheduler operates over the message set Γ applying any on-line policy and builds a single global ready queue, serializing messages according to their priority, either static or dynamic. This queue is used to build each EC-schedule that will be encoded in the TM and broadcast through the network every EC. The TM will cause all nodes that are senders in this EC to feed the scheduled packets to the network to a set of M upload links or uplinks l u j . Streams sent by each node are queued locally for transmission. Upon arrival at the switch the streams are conveyed, with latency ε, to the respective output ports and queued for transmission in the M download links or downlinks l d j (Fig. 4). However, in order to exploit as much as possible the parallel forwarding paths available in the switch, when dispatching, i.e., when building each EC-schedule, the protocol attempts to fill up the uplinks and downlinks in each EC. This methodology approximates the scheduling model to a link-oriented scheduling. The global ready queue is parsed in several ready queues, one per link (uplink or downlink), with the messages that traverse that link. The scheduler operates quasi-independently on each link with the restriction of scheduling messages together, in the same EC, in the uplinks and the downlinks. This is because we wish every message submitted to the switch in one EC to be flushed out of the switch in the same EC so that there is no traffic accumulation inside the switch from one EC to the next.

When building each EC-schedule, the scheduler fetches the messages from the uplinks queues and checks for each message whether the respective uplink and downlink in that EC are already full, using the window confinement rules specified before. When the capacity of the synchronous window in that EC is exhausted in one link, be it uplink or downlink, that link is locked in that EC and any unscheduled messages using it are left in the global ready queue. The process goes on until there are no more messages that can be scheduled in that EC.

div.head: Testing schedulability
div.p: In this section we consider two situations in terms of the number of different destinations a given node sends to. Both scenarios rely on unicast transmission and for each we present a schedulability bound that, when met, guarantees all periodic message streams to reach their destinations within their periods.

div.head: One source to one destination, only
div.p: We consider first this simple but frequent situation in which all the packets in one node are all addressed to one destination, only. However, the same destination can receive from different sources. The downlinks are in this case the bottleneck in terms of guaranteeing the system timeliness. In this case, the schedulability of the system is checked with the test in (5) applied to the downlinks.
div.formula: ∀ j mi∈l d j C i T i ≤ U lub RM,EDF × LSW -max(C i ) E(5)
div.p: The rationale behind this test is that the model considers a strictly periodic generation of messages in the uplinks thus, schedulability under RM or EDF can be checked with an utilization test similar to (4), for the uplinks. In the downlinks two situations may occur. (i) The downlink receives from just one uplink. In this case its traffic pattern matches the corresponding uplink and thus testing the downlink is enough and test (5) applies. (ii) The downlink receives from several uplinks. In this case the load of each of the uplinks is merged in the downlink but keeping the periodic release pattern. Hence, analyzing the downlink is enough to guarantee the schedulability in the corresponding uplinks. Moreover, there is no queuing inside the switch (across ECs) and the scheduling criterion, be it RM or EDF, is strictly enforced at an EC scale. The uplinks always have similar or lower load and need not to be tested, thus test (5) also applies.

div.head: One source sending to multiple destinations
div.p: This is a more general and complex situation, since the downlinks can now exhibit deferred release with jitter, which prevents the direct use of the existing utilizationbased tests as in the previous case. Despite the existence of several analysis that take release jitter into account, such analysis are response-time based, thus hard to use online and particularly for dynamic QoS distribution. We will herein provide an adequate utilization-based test that incorporates the release jitter as a new virtual task in the system. The schedulability test for this scenario is, then, the one in (6).
div.formula: ∀ j                        mi∈l u j C i T i ≤ U lub RM,EDF × LSW -max(C i ) E mi∈l d j C i T i real load + max mi∈l d j J i min mi∈l d j T i virtual load ≤ U lub RM,EDF × LSW -max(C i ) E(6)
div.p: The upper condition is the schedulability test for the uplinks, which directly emerges from (4). The lower condition applies to the downlinks that may now exhibit deferred packet releases. We conjecture that the impact of the deferred release is upper bounded by that of an extra message with transmission time equal to the maximum release delay and occurring at the frequency of the fastest message in the set of that downlink. The scheduling condition for the downlinks includes the load of all messages forward to each downlink (real load), plus the extra load due to release jitter (indirect load). Together, both components represent, what we named as, the virtual load in the downlink. The proof for this test is presented in the following section.

div.head: Utilization bounds with release jitter
div.p: Here we present the new utilization bounds for RM and EDF scheduling for general periodic and preemptive task sets with release jitter. For the sake of generality, the theorems use a terminology such as task (τ ) referring to message and execution time referring to transmission time. These bounds directly support the lower schedulability condition in (6), after applying the IIT compensation factor to the strict synchronous window confinement ((LSW -max(C i ))/E).
div.formula: Theorem 1. A preemptive task set Γ ≡ {τ i (C i , T i , J i ) , i = 1..n} with D i = T i is schedu- lable under RM if: ∀ i=1..n i j=1 C j T j + max j=1..i J j T i ≤ U lub RM (i)(7)
div.p: Proof: In this model, the worst-case situation occurs when all tasks suffer the maximum release delay and are activated all at the same time and from then on, all following activations suffer no release delay [8]. Consider that t = 0 corresponds to the periodic activation of some generic task τ i that is released J i later, in a worst-case interference scenario, illustrated in Fig. 5 (top). Under these circumstances, the response time of task τ i is upper bounded by the earliest instant t after t = J i that satisfies the following equation (Rwc i ):
div.formula: Rwc i = min t>Ji : t = i-1 j=1 t -J i + J j T j C j + C i + J i(8)
div.p: Let us now advance the time scale so that t = 0 will coincide with the earliest virtual periodic arrival among all tasks with priority equal to or higher than τ i , i.e., t → t = t + max j=1..i J j -J i . In this situation, the response time Rwc i is now given by:
div.formula: Rwc i = min t >maxj=1..i Jj : t = i-1 j=1 t -max k=1..i J k + J j T j C j + C i + max j=1..i J j (9)
div.p: Since t -max j=1..i J j = t -J i , we can conclude that Rwc i ≥ Rwc i .
The sum can be upper bounded by replacing J j with max j=1..i J j . Let Rwc i be the solution to the equation:
div.formula: Rwc i = earliest t > max j=1..i J j : i-1 j=1 t T j C j + C i + max j=1..i J j = t (10)
div.p: Necessarily, Rwc i ≥ Rwc i ≥ Rwc i . However, this last equation corresponds to a response time equation of a set of periodic tasks, without release jitter, but with task τ i inflated to C i + max j=1..i J j . This transformation is shown in Fig. 5. Thus, if this adapted task set is schedulable, so is the original task set with release jitter.
Finally, since the transformed task set is purely periodic, the Liu and Layland's utilization-based schedulability test applies [12], which proves the theorem.
div.formula: Corollary 1. A preemptive task set Γ ≡ {τ i (C i , T i , J i ) , i = 1..n} with D i = T i is schedula- ble under RM if: n i=1 C i T i + max i=1..n J i T 1 ≤ U lub RM (n)(11)
div.p: Proof:
div.formula: Just note that ∀ i , max j=1..i (J j )/T i ≤ max j=1..n (J j )/T 1 , ∀ i , U lub RM (i) ≥ U lub RM (n) Theorem 2. A preemptive task set Γ ≡ {τ i (C i , T i , J i ) , i = 1..n} is schedulable under EDF if: ∀ i=1..n i j=1 C j T j + max j=1..i J j T i ≤ U lub EDF = 1(12)
div.p: Proof: With this model, the worst-case situation in terms of highest consecutive processor demand also occurs in a similar manner as in the previous theorem [28]. The situation is also illustrated in Fig. 6 (top), in which all tasks are released as late as possible and all at the same instant. Let us define such instant as t = 0. Then, following a processor demand approach, this set is schedulable if:
div.formula: ∀ t , h(t) = i:(Ti-Ji)≤t t + J i T i C i ≤ t ⇔ ∀ t , h(t) + max i=1..n J i ≤ t + max i=1..n J i(13)
div.p: Now, let us carry out a scale shift making t = 0 coincide with the earliest virtual periodic arrival, i.e., t → t = t + max i=1..n J i . The previous schedulability condition can be written as:
div.formula: t , h(t -max i=1..n J i ) + max i=1..n J i ≤ t ⇔ i:(Ti-Ji+ max j=1..n Jj )≤t     t -max j=1..n (J j )+J i T i     C i + max j=1..n (J j ) ≤ t(14)
div.p: Again, the sum is upper bounded by replacing J i with max j=1..n J j . Thus, the following condition implies the previous one and still guarantees task set schedulability.
div.formula: ∀ t , i:T i≤t t T i C i + max j=1..n (J i ) ≤ t
div.p: In order to obtain an utilization-based expression we divide both sides by t leading to:
div.formula: ∀ t , i:T i≤t t T i C i t + max j=1..n (J i ) t ≤ 1 Observe that, t T i ≤ t T i ⇒ t T i C i t ≤ C i t × t T i = C i T i (as C i t ≥ 0)
div.p: Therefore, the term inside the sum is upper bounded by C i /T i . Thus, the following condition also implies the previous and still guarantees task set schedulability.

div.p: This condition needs to be evaluated at the instants in which t is an integer multiple of any of the tasks periods. This is particularly relevant for T 1 ≤ t ≤ T n . Within this interval, each time t reaches the first period of any task, say τ i , the corresponding term C i /T i is included in the sum. At the same time, the term max j=1..n J j /T i becomes lower as i grows since the set is sorted by ascending periods. For t > T n , the left term in the condition decreases monotonically and the condition is trivially verified if it was verified in the previous interval.

div.head: Upper bounding the indirect load
div.p: Inequalities in ( 7) and ( 12), for RM and EDF respectively, are computed considering the real load and the indirect load. However, while the first term can be directly determined from the utilization load of each task, the second one (indirect load) that represents the release jitter interference still needs to be computed. We now propose a test that aims at upper bounding this indirect load in a way to become utilization-based.
We have seen that the indirect load denotes the impact of an additional task with a load given by U ind i (Eq. 17).
div.formula: U ind i = max j=1..i J j T i , ∀i = 1..n = max j=1..i J j T i(17)
div.p: For simplicity let U ind i,j = J j T i be the interference caused by the j th task (τ j ) on τ i . Fig. 7 illustrates one such task for which the load is U ind i,j .

Coming back to the switch case with FTT-SE, remember that the release jitter that affects message m j in its downlink is a consequence of messages in the same uplink that interfere with it and are transmitted to other downlinks. Call C RM j and C EDF j the set of such messages for RM and EDF scheduling, respectively. For each case, we can also express J j as the sum of the transmission times of the interfering messages leading to an indirect load that can be expressed as in (18) for RM and EDF.
div.formula: U ind RM/EDF i,j = m k ∈C RM/EDF j Jj T k C k T i(18)
div.p: , where
div.formula: C RM j ≡ ∀m k :    S k =Sj R k =Rj k<j , C EDF j ≡ ∀m k : S k =Sj R k =Rj
div.p: Knowing that J j < T i -C i < T i an upper bound to the interfering load is given by (19), as follows 1 :
div.formula: U ind i,j < m k ∈Cj T i T k C k T i < m k ∈Cj T i T k + 1 C k T i = m k ∈Cj C k T k + m k ∈Cj C k T i(19)
div.p: Thus, we obtain the schedulability test in (20) for RM and EDF. The test must be performed for each message m i of each downlink.
div.formula: ∀ i=1..n i j=1 U j + max j=1..i   m k ∈Cj U k + m k ∈Cj C k T i   ≤ ≤ U lub (i) LSW -max ∀i (C i ) E(20)
div.p: This test, that requires the verification of n conditions, can be simplified to one condition per downlink, upper bounding the terms in the sums leading to one test that contains one single condition (Eqs. 21).
div.formula: mi∈l d j U i + max mi∈l d j    m k ∈C RM/EDF i U k    + + max mi∈l d j    m k ∈C RM/EDF i C k    T 1 ≤ ≤ U lub RM/EDF LSW -max ∀i (C i ) E(21)
div.p: This test only contains additive utilization terms thus being particularly well suited to our purpose of supporting dynamic bandwidth-based QoS management. It can thus replace the lower condition in (6) to assess the schedulability of downlink j.

div.head: Simulation results
div.p: To validate the schedulability tests, we carried out simulations with randomly generated message sets considering the following parameters:

1 For the sake of clarity we omit the RM/EDF superscripts. The message sets were pseudo-randomly generated with a virtual load per link around the theoretical schedulability bound, in order to have schedulable and nonschedulable sets. Recall the concepts of real load and virtual load as shown in Equation 6. To build a message set, random messages are sequentially added to the set while keeping the virtual load on each link under a given value, say x Mbps. After 1000 consecutive failed attempts, i.e, causing an excess to the desired load, the filling procedure is finished, guaranteeing that the virtual load is less than x Mbps and yet very close to that limit on most of the links (mainly in the downlinks that tend to reach the limit before, given the interference load). The real load in the downlinks is typically much lower than the corresponding virtual load.

The simulation was conducted through the LCM of the periods with a synchronous release and the percentage of schedulable sets was plotted as a function of the maximum virtual load (x Mbps). The following plots were obtained forcing the maximum allowed virtual load per link. They also show the Liu and Layland schedulability bounds for RM and EDF, after the inserted idle time compensation factor, which become 61% and 88%, respectively. Note that the analysis only guarantees positive schedulability results when the virtual load in all links is below these thresholds. The points of virtual load larger than the schedulability bounds with 100% schedulable sets is a measure of the pessimism that is implicit in the analysis. Fig. 8 shows the case of one destination per source, i.e., messages from one uplink go all to the same downlink, for which schedulability test in (5) applies. In this case, the virtual load coincides with the real load which is necessarily less than the links capacity of 100 Mbps. These results are similar to those for RM and EDF scheduling in one CPU, as expected, showing close to optimal performance for EDF (93 Mbps actually schedulable against the test bound of 88 Mbps) and a larger deviation from optimal for RM (79 Mbps against 61 Mbps respectively).

Fig. 9 shows the cases of 2 and 3 destinations per source with the impact of interference included in the virtual load, which can now grow beyond the link capacity of 100%. As shown in the plots, positive scheduling results are obtained with virtual load beyond the 100 Mbps of the link capacity. This happens because the considered worst-case scenario for the interference in the uplinks may never occur in practice. Note that the real load is much smaller, not exceeding the physical limits as illustrated also in Fig. 9 (dotted plot).

In all scenarios plotted in Fig. 9, the first deadline misses (with growing utilization) occur for message sets with a maximum virtual load above the 61 Mbps and 88 Mbps schedulability bounds of RM and EDF scheduling, respectively. No violation of these bounds was found, considering the maximum virtual utilization per link, confirming the schedulability analysis. The first deadline misses occur for virtual loads of 89 Mbps and 97 Mbps, for RM and EDF, respectively.

The number of schedulable sets beyond the proposed scheduling bounds reveals the bounds schedulability penalty. There are three sources for this penalty, the one already included in Liu and Layland's RM test, the intra-EC inserted idle time compensation and the interference term max i (J i )/ min i (T i ) in the downlinks. For EDF scheduling only the two latter factors apply, thus resulting in a lower degree of pessimism. This is confirmed by the simulations observing the difference between the first non-schedulable sets and the respective bounds, which is 28 Mbps for RM and 9 Mbps for EDF.

In Fig. 9 we may also observe that when increasing the diversity of destinations per source (range of downlinks per uplink) the scheduling penalty also grows. This is revealed by the observation that with the scenario of 3 possible destinations (1->3) there are more schedulable sets beyond the bounds than with the scenario of 2 possible destinations (1->2). In fact, with more downlinks per uplink the number of uplinks interfering in a downlink may grow and thus we are increasing the chance for a higher term max i (J i )/ min i (T i ) in (6). Moreover, the impact of the deferred release on each downlink is more visible at run-time when all interfering uplinks are sending to different downlinks, which, for a higher diversity of downlinks per uplink, is more likely to happen.

div.head: Future work
div.p: Beyond the practical value of the specific contribution of this paper, it is worth saying that this work is part of a larger framework to provide adaptability and reconfigurability to real-time distributed embedded systems with timeliness guarantees and robustness with respect to noncooperative or even malicious behavior from the nodes.

This work provides a substantial contribution on this regard with a schedulability test that is based on a utilization bound which is faster and more liable supporting dynamic QoS management than other known analysis techniques, such as response-time based tests. The exact-case characterization and comparison with such techniques will be carried out as future work.

The support for multicast/broadcast traffic is also required for certain applications. Such traffic poses additional interfering sources that must be accounted for, mainly the interference that downlinks may cause on each other due to the limitations posed by the use of COTS switches. In this protocol, the outgoing multicast/broadcast packets need to be processed within one single EC, establishing a constraint that complicates the scheduling of the various links and possibly making the scheduling non-work-conserving. This can only be efficiently solved with a modified switch that can schedule the multiple instances of a multicast/broadcast message separately, thus possibly being transmitted in different ECs.

It is also planned a substantial comparison study illustrating the major benefits and applicability of this lineartime schedulability analysis technique over other pseudopolynomial time schedulability analysis such as RTA and general purpose analysis techniques such as Network Calculus, on a practical case-study with dynamic reconfiguration scenarios.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Switched Ethernet is commonly found in the backbone networks of large-scale distributed real-time sys-tems, such as aircrafts, ships, trains, factories, process control plants, etc. Beyond the requirements for timeliness, there is a growing interest towards adaptability and reconfigurability as a way to facilitate system deployment, usage and maintenance, while improving resource efficiency. However, despite all the work developed in the last couple of decades on real-time communication over switched Ethernet, a few problems subsist related to queue management policies, queue overflows and limited priority support. The FTT-SE protocol was recently proposed to solve such problems providing, in particular, support for arbitrary real-time scheduling policies. In this paper we exploited this feature to realize RM and EDF scheduling in switched Ethernet and we have provided adequate utilization-based schedulability tests. In particular, we provided a theoretical contribution consisting of a set of utilization-based schedulability tests that consider the interference on a periodic task caused by release jitter in general. This result was then applied within the FTT-SE framework. Within this scope, we also proposed a way to upper bound the release jitter affecting the messages in the downlinks of the Ethernet switches under FTT-SE. The proposed tests, altogether, due to their very low time-complexity, can be quickly performed on-line in dynamic environments and thus they can be fundamental building blocks to realize dynamic bandwidth-based QoS management, either for dynamic reconfiguration or adaptation purposes. We also assessed the efficiency of proposed schedulability tests using simulations and the results show that the proposed linear-time utilization-based schedulability tests achieve within 5% utilization of the ideal test for EDF and 18% utilization of the ideal test for RMS. These values indicate a sufficiently low pessimism to grant applicability in practice.
